extracted.intended_audience: philosophers, moralists, and writers of practical ethics; educated readers and statesmen
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing moral philosophy that is both descriptive (the nature of good) and practical (the husbandry or cultivation of the mind), aimed at producing works that instruct and prompt action rather than merely entertain. Emphasises diagnostics (characters, affections), prescriptions (applications, cures), and style suited to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: instruct and suborn action
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write at leisure that men may read at leisure, but really to instruct and suborn action and active life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical works (the 'Georgics of the mind') should aim to produce practical change and application in readers' lives, not merely elegant or leisurely reading. Emphasise applicability and mobilisation toward action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold division of moral knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide moral knowledge into the exemplar or platform of good (describing the nature of good) and the regiment or culture of the mind (prescribing rules how to subdue, apply, and accommodate the will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat both description (what good is) and practical regimen (how to cultivate it) — a complete moral treatise must handle both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult nature; avoid prolixity and confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating the roots of good and evil, consult with nature to make doctrines less prolix and more profound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise clear, natural inquiry into causes and roots rather than long, diffuse disputation. Ground theory in observable nature and avoid unnecessary verbosity or confused handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public/communicative good over private good
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the double nature of good (as total and as part): the good tending to conservation of a greater form (public/communicative good) is in degree the greater and worthier than private good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical evaluation and prescriptions should weigh communal duties and the conservation of larger forms more highly than purely private advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must inform action; contemplation alone insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemplation finished in itself, without casting beams upon society, is not sufficient; moral philosophy must bear upon society and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing purely contemplative works that do not have practical consequences; even contemplative practice in religious contexts should serve public ends (prayer, instruction, prophecy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle comparative degrees and conflicts of good
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat comparative questions (e.g., contemplative vs active life, honesty vs profit, virtue vs virtue) and weigh duties between person and person, case and case, particular and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide frameworks for resolving conflicts and comparative duties; acknowledge cases where goods conflict and offer principled guidance (e.g., prefer present justice over uncertain future gains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'husbandry' (practical regimen) as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral knowledge must be accompanied by the husbandry that belongeth thereunto — methods to apply and cultivate virtue; otherwise the knowledge is like a statue beautiful to contemplate but without life and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicate explicit, written inquiry to the practical methods of reforming life (applications, exercises, cures), not only to theoretical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what is in our power vs what is not
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical ethics cast up our account what is in our power (to be altered) and what is not (to be accommodated); points of Nature and points of Fortune limit our work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design remedies and applications according to whether circumstances are alterable or must be accepted and adapted to; practice 'wise and industrious suffering' where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact knowledge of precedent state or disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The wisdom of application rests principally in the exact and distinct knowledge of the precedent state or disposition unto which we do apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before prescribing remedies or regimen, first diagnose accurately the current constitution, temper, and conditions of the person or situation (take measure before fitting the garment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic classification of characters and tempers
rubrics_metrics.description: Set down sound and true distributions and descriptions of the several characters and tempers of men's natures and dispositions, especially those differences most radical in being the fountains and causes of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide robust typologies (e.g., magnanimity vs pusillanimity, longanimity, dispositions to soothe or contradict) and derive concrete precepts for each type rather than only passing observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inherent and external impressions on character
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider impressions of Nature (sex, age, region, health, beauty) and extern fortune (sovereignty, nobility, riches, adversity) which shape dispositions and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate social, biological, and circumstantial factors into ethical diagnostics and prescriptions; these grounds are essential to practical moral philosophy, as knowledge of constitutions is to medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study affections (perturbations) as principal subject and diseases of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: After knowing characters, inquire into the diseases and infirmities of the mind (the perturbations and distempers of the affections) — these are the principal subject of medicining the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ample, active descriptions and observations of emotions and passions (not mere subtle definitions), and propose cures/remedies; treat affections distinctly from general pleasure/pain analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the frauds and vices of professions seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle frauds, cautels, impostures, and vices of every profession seriously and wisely, not merely by satire and derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose corrupt practices and deceitful arts in order to fence and fortify honesty—knowing the forms of evil is a precondition for effective moral action and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid professional bias and magnification of one's vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers speaking in their own professions commonly exalt them in excess; avoid this vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for impartiality and humility when writing about one's own vocation; specialist authors should not overvalue their field to the detriment of truth and practical usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: clarity, sobriety, and fitness for action
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should not be distempered in the heat of invention, nor in the coldness of negligence; not sick of dizziness, nor of convulsions; not savouring of perfumes and paintings; chiefly well disposed in the spirits thereof, being agreeable to truth and apt for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a sober, clear, and balanced style that avoids excessive ornament or erratic structure; aim for temperate expression that is suitable for instructing action and governance rather than mere rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should aim to learn what men do, not only what they ought
rubrics_metrics.description: We are beholden to writers who write what men do, and not what they ought to do; knowing the serpent's nature (evils) is necessary to fence virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend empirical, historical, and practical observation of human behavior into ethical theory so prescriptions engage with real conditions and resist naive simplicity.
